doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Sitting in with the Jazztet at Birdland and being hired
summary: Cedar Walton invited him to sit in; Art Farmer and Benny Golson hired him by phone the next morning as the third Jazztet, and Hampton jokingly threatened to sue.

bands.name: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: month, which wasn’t bad. Now I’m sure that same place — I go by there sometimes and look at the building — I’m sure that place probably rents for five thousand dollars a month. The same place. So I said I need a phone, so I called the phone company. First thing, “Do you have any references?” I said, “Yeah I play with Lionel Hampton’s Orchestra. They checked it out, telephone, no problem. So the gig worked that way. So now we’re getting ready to go to Wildwood, New Jersey. So Cedar Walton, one of my dearest friends, called and said, “Brother Mabern, we’re down here at Birdland with the Jazztet, you know, Art Farmer, Benny Golson, Cedar Walton, Tootie Heath and probably Tommy Williams on bass. And he says, “You might want to come and sit in” you know. And I took him on. Because I was only one stop from Birdland on the subway, you know, where I lived. So I went down and Cedar introduced me to Benny Golson. But Benny Golson and Art, they kind of knew me from Chicago anyway with the MJT + 3. So I sat in and I don’t know what we played, something kind of like here, it might have been a blues, but I started playing. See I’ve always loved to comp. That’s my passion. You know I tell people I’m more concerned about being a great comper than a great soloist, because if I comp good then I feel I have a chance to get more jobs. So I started comping and I look up and I see Benny Golson smiling you know. And Art Farmer never did show much emotion. He had his horn out here and Tommy McIntosh, yeah, he was smiling. So when he got through playing and Benny Golson said, “Yeah Mabern, man, yeah, wow.” Whatever. And Art Farmer said, “Hey man, Benny and I we really didn’t” — you know because they were very unhappy because Cedar Walton was getting ready to leave to go with Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers. Cedar Walton, Reggie Workman, Freddie Hubbard and Curtis Fuller went with that group. See that’s the thing in New York even then. Gigs were turning over. And if you happened to be in the right place you could get a gig if you could halfway play. The cat would say, “You want to sit in?” And if you could halfway play and swing, and I was always a good comper, a pretty good comper, and whatever little solo I played it swung, because I listened a lot to Wynton Kelly, one of my heroes you know. So I sat in so Art Farmer said, “Hey man, we’re getting ready to make a change and we got somebody kind of but if we hear anything we’ll let you know.” I said, “Okay, I’m going on back home to my apartment, because I’m going to Wildwood, New Jersey the next morning.” So around eight o’clock in the morning the telephone rings. I said, “Hello?” He said, “Yes, this is Art Farmer.” I said, “Yes.” I thought why is he calling me? He said, “Benny and I talked it over and we want you to join the band.” Just on the way I was comping. I’m not bragging but that’s all it was, the way I was comping and supporting them. So I said, “Well how do you want me to play?” And so Art says, “Just the way you did last night.” So at this time Benny Golson writes hard music. There are certain people that write music that write hard with a purpose: Thad

Jones, Frank Foster, Benny Golson, Slide Hampton. You know, certain ones, if I’ve got to play some of that music, get it to me ten weeks ahead of time, you know. So I told Art, I said, “Well you know Art, you know you’re playing all those hard piano parts.” So Benny said, “Don’t worry, Mabern, we’re kind of getting away from that.” Because this time, this would have been the third Jazztet from the original with McCoy Tyner. Then Cedar. Now I’m coming it and that’s the third Jazztet. So sure enough they cut back on some but I still had certain kinds of music to read. So then I got in the band so Lionel Hampton says, “Gates, I’m going to take you to court, I’m going to sue you, I told you to stay with me, I was going to make you big as bubble gum.” That was his saying, you know. But we kind of worked it out, you know, because by rights you’re supposed to give two weeks notice and I think I gave five days notice or something. Because I said at this point I can not miss this gig. I mean this is a chance to really get out in the forefront. A band from New York, be on the scene, you know what I mean? Too good to be true, you know. So but we worked it out and he wished me well because at one point in time Benny Golson and Art Farmer had both been in his band, aside from Art Blakey, Lionel Hampton had more all-stars in his band than anybody had ever had: Clifford Brown, Gigi Gryce or Quincy Jones playing trumpet, Art Farmer, Alan Dawson or Johnny Griffin.
